danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: Længe havde Rostov ikke nydt musik så meget som den dag. Men næppe havde Natasja sunget sin barcarolle færdig, før virkeligheden igen meldte sig. Han rejste sig uden et ord og gik ned til sit eget værelse. Et kvarter senere kom den gamle greve hjem fra sin klub, munter og tilfreds. Da Nikolaj hørte vognen komme, gik han ham i møde.
»Nå — har du haft det godt?« sagde den gamle greve og smilede glad og stolt til sin søn.
Nikolaj forsøgte at sige »ja«, men kunne ikke, og han var lige ved at briste i gråd. Greven var ved at tænde sin pibe og lagde ikke mærke til sin søns tilstand.

»Det kan ikke undgås!« tænkte Nikolaj for første og sidste gang. Og pludselig sagde han i den mest ligegyldige tone, som fik ham til at skamme sig over sig selv, som om han blot bad sin far om at få vognen til at køre til byen:
»Far, jeg kommer i et ærinde. Jeg havde næsten glemt det. Jeg har brug for nogle penge.«
»Jamen dog!« sagde hans far, der var i særlig godt humør. »Jeg sagde jo, det ikke ville slå til. Hvor meget?«
»Meget,« sagde Nikolaj og rødmede, med et dumt, tankeløst smil, som han længe ikke kunne tilgive sig selv. »Jeg har tabt lidt, jeg mener en del, rigtig meget — treogfyrre tusind.«
»Hvad! Til hvem? ... Vrøvl!« råbte greven og rødmede pludselig med det apoplektiske skær over hals og nakke, som ældre mennesker gør.
»Jeg har lovet at betale i morgen,« sagde Nikolaj.
»Nå ja! ...« sagde den gamle greve, bredte armene ud og sank hjælpeløst ned på sofaen.

»Det kan ikke hjælpes! Det sker for alle!« sagde sønnen med en modig, fri og let tone, mens han i sin sjæl betragtede sig selv som en værdiløs slyngel, hvis hele liv ikke kunne sone hans forbrydelse. Han længtes efter at kysse sin fars hænder og knæle ned og bede om tilgivelse, men sagde med en tankeløs og ligefrem grov stemme, at det sker for alle!
Den gamle greve slog øjnene ned, da han hørte sin søns ord, og begyndte travlt at lede efter noget.
»Ja, ja,« mumlede han, »det bliver svært, frygter jeg, svært at skaffe ... sker for alle! Ja, hvem har ikke gjort det?«
Og med et flygtigt blik på sin søns ansigt gik greven ud af værelset ... Nikolaj havde været forberedt på modstand, men havde slet ikke ventet dette.
»Far! Fa-ar!« kaldte han efter ham, hulkende. »Tilgiv mig!« Og idet han greb sin fars hånd, pressede han den mod sine læber og brast i gråd.
Mens far og søn havde deres forklaring, havde mor og datter en ikke mindre vigtig. Natasja kom løbende ind til sin mor, helt ophidset.
»Mama! ... Mama! ... Han har friet ...«
»Friet hvad?«
»Friet, friet til mig, mama! Mama!« udbrød hun.
Grevinden troede ikke sine egne ører. Denisov havde friet. Til hvem? Til dette pigebarn, Natasja, der for ikke så længe siden legede med dukker og stadig gik til undervisning.
»Lad være, Natasja! Sikke noget vrøvl!« sagde hun og håbede, det var en spøg.
»Vrøvl? Jeg fortæller dig, hvad der er sket, og du kalder det vrøvl!« sagde Natasja indigneret.
Grevinden trak på skuldrene.
»Hvis det er sandt, at Monsieur Denisov har friet til dig, så sig til ham, at han er en nar, og dermed basta!«
»Nej, han er ikke en nar!« svarede Natasja indigneret og alvorligt.
»Nå, hvad vil du så? I er jo alle forelskede for tiden. Jamen, hvis du er forelsket, så gift dig med ham!« sagde grevinden med et irriteret grin. »Held og lykke!«
»Nej, mama, jeg er ikke forelsket i ham, det tror jeg ikke.«
»Nå, så sig ham det.«
»Mama, er du vred? Vær nu ikke vred, søde! Er det min skyld?«
»Nej, men hvad er det, min pige? Vil du have, at jeg går ind og siger det til ham?« sagde grevinden smilende.

»Nej, det gør jeg selv, bare fortæl mig, hvad jeg skal sige. Det er nemt nok for dig,« sagde Natasja med et gengældt smil. »Du skulle have set, hvordan han sagde det! Jeg ved, han ikke mente at sige det, men det kom bare ud af sig selv.«
»Nå, men du må afvise ham alligevel.«
»Nej, det kan jeg ikke. Jeg har så ondt af ham! Han er så sød.«
»Jamen, så tag imod hans frieri. Det er på høje tid, du bliver gift,« svarede grevinden skarpt og sarkastisk.
»Nej, mama, men jeg har så ondt af ham. Jeg ved ikke, hvad jeg skal sige.«
»Du behøver ikke sige noget. Jeg taler selv med ham,« sagde grevinden, oprørt over, at de havde vovet at behandle lille Natasja som voksen.

»Nej, under ingen omstændigheder! Jeg siger det selv, og du lytter ved døren,« og Natasja løb tværs over dagligstuen hen til danseværelset, hvor Denisov sad på den samme stol ved klaveret med ansigtet i hænderne.
Han sprang op ved lyden af hendes lette trin.
»Natalja,« sagde han og bevægede sig med hurtige skridt hen imod hende, »afgør min skæbne. Den er i dine hænder.«
»Vasilij Dmitritj, jeg har så ondt af Dem! ... Nej, men De er så rar ... men det går ikke ... ikke på den måde ... men som ven, vil jeg altid holde af Dem.«

Denisov bøjede sig over hendes hånd, og hun hørte mærkelige lyde, hun ikke forstod. Hun kyssede hans stride, krøllede, sorte hoved. I det øjeblik hørtes den hurtige raslen af grevindens kjole. Hun kom hen til dem.

»Vasilij Dmitritj, jeg takker Dem for den ære,« sagde hun med forlegen stemme, skønt den lød streng for Denisov, »men min datter er så ung, og jeg troede, at De som min søns ven først ville have henvendt Dem til mig. I så fald ville De ikke have tvunget mig til at give dette afslag.«
»Grevinde ...« sagde Denisov med nedslagne øjne og skyldbevidst ansigt. Han forsøgte at sige mere, men stammede.
Natasja kunne ikke beherske sig ved synet af ham i en sådan tilstand. Hun begyndte at hulke højlydt.

»Grevinde, jeg har handlet forkert,« fortsatte Denisov med usikker stemme, »men tro mig, jeg tilbeder Deres datter og hele Deres familie så meget, at jeg ville give mit liv to gange ...« Han så på grevinden, og da han så hendes strenge ansigt, sagde han: »Nå, farvel, grevinde,« og kyssede hendes hånd og forlod værelset med hurtige, beslutsomme skridt uden at se på Natasja.

Næste dag tog Rostov afsked med Denisov. Han ønskede ikke at blive i Moskva endnu en dag. Alle Denisovs moskovitiske venner gav ham en afskedsfest hos sigøjnerne, med det resultat, at han intet kunne huske om, hvordan han blev sat op i kanen, eller om de tre første stationer af rejsen.

Efter Denisovs afrejse tilbragte Rostov endnu to uger i Moskva uden at forlade huset, mens han ventede på de penge, hans far ikke straks kunne skaffe, og det meste af tiden sad han i pigernes værelse.

Sonja var mere øm og hengiven over for ham end nogensinde. Det var, som om hun ville vise ham, at hans tab var en bedrift, der fik hende til at elske ham endnu mere, men Nikolaj betragtede nu sig selv som uværdig til hende.

Han fyldte pigernes albums med vers og musik, og efter endelig at have sendt Dolokhov de fulde treogfyrre tusind rubler og modtaget hans kvittering rejste han i slutningen af november uden at tage afsked med nogen af sine bekendte for at indhente sit regiment, der allerede var i Polen.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It had been a long time since Rostov had enjoyed music as much as he did that day. But the moment Natasha finished her barcarolle, reality came crashing back. He got up without a word and went downstairs to his own room. Fifteen minutes later the old count came home from his club, cheerful and pleased with himself. Nicholas, hearing the carriage pull up, went to meet him.
"Well — did you have a good time?" said the old count, beaming proudly at his son.
Nicholas tried to say "Yes," but could barely get the word out — he nearly burst into sobs. The count was lighting his pipe and didn't notice his son's state.

"It can't be helped!" thought Nicholas, for the first and last time. And suddenly, in the most casual tone he could manage — a tone that made him ashamed of himself — he said, as if merely asking his father for the carriage to go into town:
"Papa, I've come about a matter of business. I nearly forgot. I need some money."
"Oh dear!" said his father, who was in an especially good mood. "I told you it wouldn't be enough. How much?"

"Quite a lot," said Nicholas, flushing, and with a stupid, careless smile for which he could never forgive himself afterward. "I've lost a little — I mean a good deal, a great deal — forty-three thousand."
"What! To whom? Nonsense!" cried the count, suddenly reddening with a rush of blood to his neck and the back of his head, the way old men do.
"I promised to pay tomorrow," said Nicholas.
"Well!" said the old count, spreading out his arms and sinking helplessly onto the sofa.

"It can't be helped! It happens to everyone!" said the son in a bold, offhand tone, while deep in his soul he saw himself as a worthless scoundrel whose entire life couldn't make up for his crime. He longed to kiss his father's hands and beg forgiveness on his knees, yet he spoke in a careless, even rude voice, saying that it happens to everyone!
The old count dropped his eyes at his son's words and began frantically searching around for something.
"Yes, yes," he muttered, "it'll be hard, I'm afraid — hard to raise... happens to everybody! Yes, who hasn't done it?"
And with a furtive glance at his son's face, the count left the room. Nicholas had been prepared for resistance, but had not at all expected this.
"Papa! Papa!" he called after him, sobbing. "Forgive me!" And seizing his father's hand, he pressed it to his lips and burst into tears.
While father and son were having this conversation, the mother and daughter were having one no less important. Natasha came running to her mother, breathless with excitement.
"Mama! Mama! He's made me..."
"Made what?"
"Made me — he's proposed, Mama! Mama!" she exclaimed.
The countess couldn't believe her ears. Denisov had proposed. To whom? To this slip of a girl, Natasha, who not long ago was playing with dolls and was still having lessons.
"Don't be silly, Natasha! What nonsense!" she said, hoping it was a joke.
"Nonsense indeed! I'm telling you it's true," said Natasha indignantly. "I've come to ask you what to do, and you call it 'nonsense!'"
The countess shrugged her shoulders.
"If it's true that Monsieur Denisov has proposed to you, tell him he's a fool — that's all!"
"No, he's not a fool!" replied Natasha, indignant and serious.
"Well then, what do you want? You're all in love these days. Fine — if you're in love, marry him!" said the countess with an annoyed laugh. "Good luck to you!"
"No, Mama, I'm not in love with him. I don't think I'm in love with him."
"Well then, tell him so."
"Mama, are you angry? Don't be angry, darling! Is it my fault?"
"No, but what is all this, my dear? Do you want me to go tell him?" said the countess with a smile.

"No, I'll do it myself — just tell me what to say. It's easy for you," said Natasha, smiling back. "You should have seen how he said it! I know he didn't mean to say it — it just slipped out accidentally."
"Well, all the same, you must refuse him."
"No, I can't. I feel so sorry for him! He's so nice."
"Well then, accept his proposal. It's high time you were married," the countess answered sharply and sarcastically.
"No, Mama, but I feel so sorry for him. I don't know how to say it."
"And there's nothing for you to say. I'll speak to him myself," said the countess, indignant that anyone should dare treat this little Natasha as a grown-up.

"No, absolutely not! I'll tell him myself, and you can listen at the door," and Natasha ran through the drawing room to the ballroom, where Denisov sat on the same chair by the clavichord with his face in his hands.
He jumped up at the sound of her light step.
"Nataly," he said, rushing toward her with quick steps, "decide my fate. It is in your hands."
"Vasili Dmitrich, I feel so sorry for you! No, but you are so nice... but it won't do... not that... but as a friend, I will always love you."

Denisov bent over her hand, and she heard strange sounds she didn't understand. She kissed his rough, curly black head. At that instant they heard the quick rustle of the countess's dress. She came up to them.

"Vasili Dmitrich, I thank you for the honor," she said in an embarrassed voice that sounded severe to Denisov, "but my daughter is so young, and I would have thought that, as my son's friend, you would have spoken to me first. In that case you would not have forced me to give this refusal."
"Countess..." said Denisov, with downcast eyes and a guilty expression. He tried to say more but faltered.
Natasha could not bear seeing him in such distress. She began to sob aloud.

"Countess, I was wrong," Denisov continued in an unsteady voice, "but believe me, I adore your daughter and all your family so much that I would give my life twice over..." He looked at the countess, and seeing her stern face said: "Well, goodbye, Countess," and kissing her hand, he strode out of the room without looking at Natasha.

The next day Rostov saw Denisov off. He didn't want to stay another day in Moscow. All of Denisov's Moscow friends gave him a farewell party at the gypsies', with the result that he had no memory of how he was put in the sleigh or of the first three stages of his journey.

After Denisov's departure, Rostov spent another two weeks in Moscow without leaving the house, waiting for the money his father couldn't raise right away, and he spent most of his time in the girls' room.

Sonya was more tender and devoted to him than ever. It was as if she wanted to show him that his losses were something noble that made her love him all the more, but Nicholas now considered himself unworthy of her.

He filled the girls' albums with verses and music, and having at last sent Dolokhov the full forty-three thousand rubles and received his receipt, he left at the end of November — without taking leave of any of his acquaintances — to rejoin his regiment, which was already in Poland.
